title: The Atomic Nucleus
description: Protons, neutrons, and the strongest force in nature

concepts.title: Nucleons
concepts.contentHtml:
The nucleus is a tightly packed collection of protons (charge +e, mass ≈ 938 MeV/c²) and neutrons (charge 0, mass ≈ 940 MeV/c²) — collectively called nucleons.

An element's identity is set by Z (proton number). Different N (neutron number) for the same Z gives different isotopes: ¹²C, ¹³C, and ¹⁴C are all carbon, but with 6, 7, and 8 neutrons.

Nuclei are tiny — radius about 1.2 × A^(1/3) fm. A whole atom is 100,000 times larger; nearly all the mass is in a near-point at the center.

concepts.title: Binding Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
A nucleus weighs slightly less than the sum of its individual nucleons. The missing mass — the mass defect — has been converted to binding energy by E = mc².

Plot binding energy per nucleon vs. mass number A and you get a curve that peaks near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV/nucleon).

This curve drives all of nuclear physics: lighter nuclei release energy by fusing toward iron; heavier nuclei release energy by fissioning toward iron.

concepts.title: The Strong Nuclear Force
concepts.contentHtml:
Protons should fly apart from electrostatic repulsion. They don't, because the strong nuclear force is much stronger over short distances.

It's actually the residual of the underlying quark-gluon strong force — the same QCD that confines quarks into nucleons. Beyond about 2 fm it's negligible; below 1 fm it overwhelms electromagnetism.

It's charge-independent: proton-proton, proton-neutron, neutron-neutron strong attractions are nearly equal.

title: Radioactive Decay
description: Alpha, beta, gamma — and the half-life

concepts.title: The Three Decay Modes
concepts.contentHtml:
Alpha decay: nucleus emits a He-4 nucleus (2p + 2n). Z drops by 2, A drops by 4. Common in heavy nuclei (uranium, radon).

Beta-minus decay: a neutron converts to a proton, electron, and antineutrino. Z increases by 1, A unchanged. Common in neutron-rich isotopes.

Gamma decay: an excited nucleus drops to lower energy by emitting a high-energy photon. No change in Z or A; just a release of stored energy.

concepts.title: Half-Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Radioactive decay is a quantum random process. For each nucleus there's a probability per unit time of decaying. With many nuclei, the population follows N(t) = N₀ e^(-λt).

The half-life t_½ = ln 2 / λ is the time for half of any sample to decay. Half-lives span an enormous range: ⁸Be ≈ 10⁻¹⁶ s; ²³⁸U ≈ 4.5 × 10⁹ years; ¹²⁸Te > 10²⁴ years.

Half-life is exquisitely set by nuclear structure — small changes in nuclear shell occupation can change a half-life by twenty orders of magnitude.

concepts.title: Radiometric Dating
concepts.contentHtml:
Half-lives are constant (within parts per billion). So the ratio of decay products to parent isotope tells you how long ago a sample was formed.

¹⁴C (t_½ ≈ 5730 yr) for organic material up to ~50,000 years. U-Pb for rocks billions of years old. K-Ar for moderate timescales.

Radiometric dating gave us the age of the Earth (4.54 ± 0.05 billion years), the timing of mass extinctions, and the chronology of human evolution. It's one of physics' biggest gifts to other sciences.

concepts.title: How Fission Works
concepts.contentHtml:
Hit a heavy nucleus like ²³⁵U with a slow neutron and it can split into two medium-mass fragments plus 2-3 free neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV of energy per fission.

The reason: the binding-energy curve. Two mid-mass fragments are more tightly bound than one heavy nucleus; the difference becomes kinetic energy.

Discovered in 1938 by Hahn and Strassmann, with the theoretical interpretation by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch within weeks.

concepts.title: Chain Reactions
concepts.contentHtml:
The neutrons released by fission can trigger more fissions. If on average more than one neutron from each fission causes another fission, you get a chain reaction.

Multiplication factor k. k = 1: critical (steady state — a reactor). k > 1: supercritical (runaway — a bomb). k < 1: subcritical (dies out).

Reactor control rods absorb neutrons to hold k right at 1. Bombs use a sudden assembly of supercritical mass to maximize energy release.

concepts.title: Reactors & Waste
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern reactors use natural or low-enriched ²³⁵U fuel, water as coolant and moderator (slows neutrons to thermal speeds where fission is most probable), and control rods of boron or cadmium.

Spent fuel contains long-lived isotopes — Pu-239, Cs-137, Sr-90 — radiotoxic for thousands of years. Disposal remains an unresolved political and engineering problem.

Newer designs (molten-salt, fast-spectrum, small modular) aim to burn waste, run safely without active cooling, and cost less.

title: Fusion
description: Powering the stars — and someday, the grid

concepts.title: Why Fusion Releases Energy
concepts.contentHtml:
Light nuclei are below the binding-energy peak at iron. Fuse two of them and the product is more tightly bound — energy released.

Fusion reaction per kilogram releases ~10× more energy than fission, and ~10⁶× more than chemical burning. Plus the fuel is essentially limitless (deuterium from seawater) and the products are non-radioactive (helium).

The catch: getting two positively-charged nuclei close enough that the strong force takes over, despite their electrostatic repulsion.

concepts.title: Stellar Fusion
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium via the p-p chain: four protons → ⁴He + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + energy.

The bottleneck step (p + p → d + e⁺ + ν) requires a weak interaction — and the weak force is so weak that this happens to any given proton only once every ~10 billion years on average. That's why the Sun burns slowly enough for life to evolve.

More massive stars use the CNO cycle, with carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen as catalysts.

concepts.title: Fusion on Earth
concepts.contentHtml:
Replicating fusion on Earth requires temperatures of 10⁸ K, hot enough that nuclei have enough kinetic energy to tunnel through the Coulomb barrier.

Magnetic confinement (tokamaks, stellarators) traps a plasma in twisted magnetic fields. Inertial confinement (NIF) blasts a fuel pellet with lasers to compress and heat it before it explodes apart.

The 2022 NIF shot was the first to release more fusion energy than the lasers delivered. ITER, a magnetic-fusion reactor in France, expects net energy gain in the 2030s. Practical fusion electricity is decades away — and has been for decades.

title: Applications & Frontier
description: Medicine, materials, and where nuclear physics is headed

concepts.title: Nuclear Medicine
concepts.contentHtml:
PET scans use a positron-emitting isotope (typically ¹⁸F) attached to a metabolic tracer. Positrons annihilate with electrons, producing back-to-back gamma rays that detectors localize.

Radiation therapy uses gamma rays or proton beams to kill tumors with high precision. Brachytherapy implants radioactive seeds. Targeted alpha therapy ties an alpha emitter to a tumor-seeking antibody.

Roughly one third of all hospital patients receive a procedure involving radioisotopes — overwhelmingly diagnostic. Technetium-99m (⁹⁹ᵐTc, from reactor-produced ⁹⁹Mo) dominates diagnostic imaging.

concepts.title: Cosmic Rays & Astrophysics
concepts.contentHtml:
The universe is a giant nuclear laboratory. Big-bang nucleosynthesis made the H, He, and trace Li in the first 20 minutes after the Big Bang. Stellar nucleosynthesis makes heavier elements through fusion and the s-process. Supernovae and neutron-star mergers make the heaviest elements via the r-process.

Cosmic rays — ultra-high-energy particles from space — provide a window into nuclear processes far beyond what accelerators can reach. Some have energies above 10²⁰ eV, ten million times the LHC.

concepts.title: Open Questions
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclear physics has plenty of unsolved problems:

• Neutrinoless double beta decay: if observed, would prove neutrinos are their own antiparticles (Majorana fermions) and shed light on matter-antimatter asymmetry.
• Nuclear equation of state: how do neutron stars (effectively giant nuclei) behave at extreme density?
• Superheavy elements: is there an 'island of stability' beyond Z = 118?
• Nuclear shell structure for exotic isotopes: shell magic numbers may shift far from stability.
